references_named: Damien Hirst, The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living (1991)
Damien Hirst, the 2006 replacement of the decomposed original shark
Walter Benjamin, The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1935)
rationale: The bfcache is genuinely the work's medium: the mechanism enacts preservation rather than illustrating it, and the reload path enacts the 2006 replacement scandal as a button. The Hirst détournement is precise, the wall label and SOLD dot carry the market critique, and the live readout honestly reports when the browser refuses to bfcache. Double-coding lands at both depths. Distinct from the catalogue: no prior work uses bfcache/freeze/resume as the literal preservation apparatus, and the Hirst reference is new to the corpus.
reservations: The shark drawing is competent but slightly illustrative rather than fully enacted; the canvas animation is decorative ballast around the real argument (the bfcache). The 'Preserved for' counter is a wall-text flourish rather than a mechanism. Craft is solid but not the smallest possible build — a pure pageshow/freeze/resume demo with no canvas would arguably be more restrained (P3).
revision_suggestion: Consider whether the shark itself is necessary, or whether the vitrine, label, and live state readout alone — with the bfcache as the only 'image' — would be more in the spirit of P3 minimal gesture. The canvas could be reduced to a single static silhouette whose only motion is the bob, making the suspension more legible.
